newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Dreading yet yearning for jobs.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Dreading yet yearning for jobs.

text.p: The U.S. credit market will finally get the data it has been alternately yearning for and dreading for weeks on Friday in the form of the August employment report.
A steady stream of robust economic data has led the market to question Federal Reserve forecasts for a second half slowdown of late.
Many believe Friday's payrolls report, due at 0830 EDT/1330 GMT, will shatter these hopes completely and force the Fed's hand come September 24.
"As always payrolls will be very important," said Lee Youngdahl, money market economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co Inc.

"In particular, it's very important for the Fed. They're possibly right on the cusp of having to reverse (the direction of) policy and going to a tightening stance so it has a great deal of import for them."
Economists surveyed by Reuters are calling for a gain of 244,000 non-farm jobs in August compared to an advance of 193,000 in July.

The average hourly eanings component of the report -- a key gauge of inflation pressures -- is expected to rise at a 0.3 percent pace, while the unemployment rate is seen edging down to 5.3 percent from 5.4 percent in the previous month.
Forecasts call for the average workweek to rise 0.2 percentage points to 34.5 hours in August.
Kathy Bostjancic, a money market analyst at UBS Securities, said the Treasury market would likely have trouble digesting a headline number showing growth in excess of 250,000.
She said a jump in hourly earnings in excess of 0.3 percent and a decline in the unemployment rate to 5.2 percent or lower would send yields higher as well.
"This number is very important," Bostjancic said. "It's among the timeliest of economic reports and it gives us information on spending, earnings and manufacturing."
If the report comes in strong enough, some economists have said they expect the Fed to hike rates even before its upcoming September 24 policy meeting.
The minutes of the July Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting showed policymakers had adopted a tightening bias which gives the leeway for an inter-meeting move.

But although economists are near unanimous in their belief that the bias was kept in place at the most recent August 20 meeting, a vast majority believe the central bank would prefer to wait until the next meeting for any move on rates, regardless of payrolls.
"I would give (an inter-meeting move) a very low probability barring a shockingly high number," said Youngdahl.

The benchmark 6.75 percent 30-year bond was off 20/32 at 95-01/32 to yield 7.15 percent in late trading on Thursday. The federal funds rate is expected to open between 5-3/16 and 5-1/4 percent on Friday.
